idiom_name: Vec<T> of records addressed by index (or generational) handles, swept by iter_mut
implementation_notes: Vec<T> is 'a contiguous growable array type' and slices are views into it, so the packed layout is Rust's default: keep records by value, address them with a handle (u32/usize or a generational index), and let ownership prevent the aliasing that pointer graphs require. What replaces the classic structure: one Vec per record type plus handles replaces webs of Rc<RefCell<..>>, and the borrow checker enforces the split between storage and iteration that data-oriented code wants anyway. Layout is explicit when it is part of the contract - the default representation may reorder fields, while #[repr(C)] fixes the C ordering algorithm and #[repr(align(N))]/#[repr(packed)] adjust padding. swap_remove keeps the active prefix packed; split_at_mut/split_first_mut let two records be borrowed at once without handle indirection.
pitfalls: The default representation may reorder fields, so anything that depends on the physical layout (FFI, serialization, a shipped hot/cold split) needs #[repr(C)] or explicit conversion.
Handles are not checked: after swap_remove or reordering, a stale index silently addresses another record - use a generational index/slot map when handles outlive the frame.
The borrow checker rejects iterating the pool while a distinct element is mutably borrowed; split the slice (split_at_mut) or index by handle instead of restructuring the data.
Vec reallocation invalidates any raw pointer or slice derived earlier; derive slices per access rather than storing them.

variants.name: Archetype column storage in an ECS crate (hecs / bevy_ecs)
variants.idiom_name: hecs::World with per-type archetype columns (ArchetypeColumn) queried as (&mut Position, &Velocity)
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of hand-maintaining parallel vectors, delegate the layout to an ECS crate: hecs describes itself as 'a high-performance, minimalist entity-component-system (ECS) world', where an Archetype is 'a collection of entities having the same component types' and an ArchetypeColumn is a reference to a single column of component data - i.e. per-component-type packed storage with an entity handle (its Entity is a 'lightweight unique ID'). What replaces the classic structure: components become plain structs stored in columns, entities are ids, and the hot loop is a query that iterates only the archetypes holding the required components, skipping entities that lack them. Choose it when the entity set is dynamic (spawn/despawn changes the archetype mix), when several systems sweep overlapping component sets, or when bevy_ecs's scheduler/parallel iteration is wanted.
pitfalls: Component types are the storage key: one component of a given type per entity, so 'two of the same' must be modelled as a collection or a distinct type.
Structural changes (spawn/despawn, add/remove component) move entities between archetypes and are deferred or restricted while a query borrow is live.
Queries borrow the world, so systems that also read other entities must go through the world API again instead of holding two overlapping borrows.
Archetype count grows with the number of distinct component combinations; a highly fragmented entity mix produces many small columns and loses the locality the crates promise.
